articles.title: Read Mayor Zohran Mamdani's statement as New York bans AI in Elementary and Middle Schools; says: Tech industry wants us to believe ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: New York City is putting strict limits on AI in public schools, with younger students facing the biggest restrictions. According to a report by New Yo.
articles.body: New York City is putting strict limits on AI in public schools, with younger students facing the biggest restrictions. According to a report by New York Times, about 600,000 students, or roughly two-thirds of the city’s public school population, will not be allowed to use AI until they reach high school, while AI use in high school will be limited to specific cases. As per the report, the policy is also placing new limits on digital devices and screen time. No individual screens will be allowed for students until third grade, while middle school students could face a recommended screen-time limit of 45 minutes a day. AI-powered companion chatbots designed to provide emotional or mental support will also be banned across all grades.Mayor Zohran Mamdani says AI in early education is not necessaryNew York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani said the city does not accept the idea that AI must become part of early education. “The tech industry wants us to believe that A.I.-powered early education is not only inevitable, but necessary. We do not see it that way,” Mamdani said in a statement as quoted in the report."I am proud to announce New York City's first-ever comprehensive AI policy for our public schools, City Hall's answer to those questions. It is the most comprehensive of its kind anywhere in the country, and it begins with a simple principle: Children need their teachers and human connection in order to learn and in order to grow. And they need to develop skills alongside their peers, build relationships with their teachers, and wrestle with tough problems on their own. The tech industry wants us to believe that AI in early education is not only inevitable but that it is necessary. We do not see it that way. I have yet to see a study showing that AI is beneficial for students in elementary and middle school, with the exception, of course, of research sponsored by the very corporations that stand to profit. So, beginning this school year, we will implement a one-year moratorium on generative AI for students in 2-K through eighth grade," Mamdani said.Schools Chancellor Kamar Samuels also said the city would not treat more technology as the same thing as innovation.“We’re putting guardrails in place to protect the critical human connection, curiosity, and creativity that help children grow,” he said.What New York's AI school rules mean for studentsUnder the new policy, AI will generally be off limits for elementary and middle school students until they enter high school. High school students will be allowed to use AI in certain situations. The rules also address how teachers can use AI. Teachers will be allowed to use AI for tasks such as creating lesson plans, translating materials and writing messages.However, AI cannot be used to make certain important decisions about students. For example, teachers cannot use AI to decide whether a student should graduate or determine how to counsel a student experiencing a crisis.The rules also include exceptions for some technology. Centrally approved instructional programs, including e-books and coding software, will not be covered by the restrictions. Some testing tools and technology designed to support students with disabilities or those learning English will also be exempt.New York schools face questions over AI-powered appsAs stated in the NYT report, the policy could also affect educational apps already used in schools, particularly as more software companies add generative AI features to their products. Naveed Hasan, a member of a city education oversight panel, questioned how the rules would work when AI is becoming part of many software products.The city education system has a budget of about $40 billion, giving it significant purchasing power when dealing with technology companies. Hasan said the department could potentially use that influence to push companies to change how their educational apps work.Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: Robert Kiyosaki, the ‘Rich Dad Poor Dad’ author, is $1.2 billion in debt: How the self-help guru uses borrowing to build wealth
articles.summary: Trending News: Robert Kiyosaki, author of 'Rich Dad Poor Dad,' owes $1.2 billion, and he says that’s a feature, not a bug. He’s made a career out of teaching people .
articles.body: Robert Kiyosaki, author of 'Rich Dad Poor Dad,' owes $1.2 billion, and he says that’s a feature, not a bug. He’s made a career out of teaching people that debt doesn’t have to be a financial disaster. In fact, he’s very public about the staggering amount he owes, explaining that debt, when used right, is core to how he built wealth. It’s a twist on the usual American dream, where most people scramble for years to wipe out their debt, not brag about it.Recently, that $1.2 billion number started making the rounds again after Kiyosaki talked about it on the Get Rich Education podcast. He’s 79 now, not slowing down, and happy to repeat that his approach isn’t something everyone should just copy. Per the New York Post, he’s been studying debt since the ’70s and still argues that borrowing, done wisely, is a tool, not a trap. But behind the shock value of that billion-dollar figure, there’s a detail most headlines miss: it’s not all unsecured debt hanging over his head. Most of it’s linked to real estate, with partners, so his personal stake is way smaller: more in the tens of millions, not a billion plus.Robert Kiyosaki’s ‘good debt’ philosophy: Why is he so unfazed by owing so much?It all comes back to one of his main ideas: debt can be good or bad, depending on what you do with it. In his world, “good debt” is when you borrow to buy something that actually puts money in your pocket, like apartments that generate rent, instead of buying stuff that just drains your cash.Real estate is the heart of how he operates. Kiyosaki doesn’t sit around waiting for decades, hoping to save enough cash to buy buildings outright. He takes out loans, acquires properties, and as those buildings pay rent and (hopefully) rise in value, he builds equity, using other people’s money. That’s the idea powering his books and seminars, and it’s what made ‘Rich Dad Poor Dad’ a monster hit. He took a simple family contrast: his own “Poor Dad” vs. his friend’s “Rich Dad” and used it to reframe how millions of people think about money.Where exactly does that infamous $1.2 billion come from?Mostly, it’s tied to a massive portfolio of apartment buildings. Together with his former wife Kim, who’s also deeply involved in his business world, they invested in something like 1,500 apartments. They own these properties with partners, so this mountain of debt isn’t on Kiyosaki’s credit card. Kim herself admitted he only owes a fraction personally, maybe $30–60 million, based on what’s been reported. It’s still a lot, but it’s a different story.Kiyosaki’s specialty is borrowing against the value of real estate. Suppose he buys a building with a mortgage, and the value rises over time. Instead of selling off and losing the asset, he borrows against the equity, pulling out cash to buy more properties. He relies on those assets generating enough income for the loans to make sense: if the rent covers the costs, it’s a win. He also points out the tax benefits: a loan isn’t taxed like income. But, and it’s a big “but,” the properties need to actually pay enough, or the whole strategy falls apart quickly. It’s much riskier than the catchy tagline “rich people use debt” makes it sound.The dark side is that leverage works both ways. It amplifies gains, but if the market swings down, like rents drop, properties lose value, vacancies rise, or interest rates spike, that same debt can crush an investor. Experts who’ve commented on Kiyosaki’s tactics always throw up a warning sign: you'd better know exactly what you’re doing. Kiyosaki himself says education comes first, so don’t just try this because you saw a viral quote.Why talk about the 'billion-dollar debt' so much?It’s not just shock value, though Kiyosaki loves a flashy number. He knows those headlines get people listening, and then he can launch into his real message about “good debt.” The soundbite exists partly to sell the story, not just to lay out a balance sheet.It’s important to get the context, though: he’s not talking about credit card debt or personal loans that keep people up at night. He’s talking about loans that are tied to assets designed to bring in money, usually shared with other investors. If anything, the headline proves his point. In Kiyosaki’s world, a gigantic debt is a badge of honor, not a sign he’s lost control. It’s his way of walking the talk and showing that, when used his way, debt can build fortunes instead of destroying them.Get the latest movie news, reviews, and celebrity updates. articles.title: An $8 million grant helped transfer 1,688 California acres to public ownership; the ranch will protect 1.6 miles of an undammed river and a major wildlife corridor
articles.summary: US News: An $8 million conservation grant has helped place 1,688 acres of California ranchland into public ownership, protecting a stretch of one of the Easter.
articles.body: An $8 million conservation grant has helped place 1,688 acres of California ranchland into public ownership, protecting a stretch of one of the Eastern Sierra’s few major undammed rivers and preserving a critical wildlife corridor. According to Alpine County, Western Rivers Conservancy and the California Wildlife Conservation Board, Park Ranch near Markleeville was formally transferred to Alpine County in August. The property includes 1.6 miles of the East Fork Carson River and nearly three miles of its tributaries. The transfer marks the end of a conservation effort that began when Western Rivers Conservancy (WRC) acquired the ranch in two phases starting in 2025. The organization has now handed the property to the county for permanent stewardship.A river left undammedThe East Fork Carson River is one of the few major rivers in the Eastern Sierra that remains undammed. The section running through Park Ranch is also valued for its trout waters and recreational opportunities.Along with the 1.6-mile stretch of the main river, the property contains about 2.97 miles of Markleeville Creek, Pleasant Valley Creek and Hot Springs Creek. These waterways provide habitat for native fish, including the federally threatened Lahontan cutthroat trout, as well as Paiute sculpin, mountain whitefish, mountain sucker, Tahoe sucker, Lahontan redside shiner and speckled dace.The ranch’s landscape includes mountain meadows, cottonwood and willow stands, mixed-conifer forests and sagebrush-steppe, a mix that makes the property particularly valuable to wildlife.A vital corridor for wildlifePark Ranch also sits within an important movement corridor used by mule deer, black bears and other wildlife as they move seasonally through the Eastern Sierra.Conservation of the property is intended to keep that corridor connected while protecting river and riparian habitat. WRC also removed sections of fencing during its ownership to improve wildlife movement and installed wildlife-friendly fencing along Markleeville Creek to reduce erosion. The $8 million grant was allocated by California’s Wildlife Conservation Board to support acquisition of the property. The board’s May 2026 agenda described the project as protecting an interconnected Eastern Sierra landscape while creating future wildlife-oriented public-use opportunities.Conservation, with a working-ranch legacyThe ranch will not simply become open space. Alpine County plans to continue compatible grazing as part of its approach to habitat management and wildfire-fuel reduction.That is significant for nearby Markleeville, where reducing vegetation that could fuel wildfires is a key concern. During WRC’s ownership, livestock grazing continued for this purpose. The property will ultimately be managed for conservation, wildlife and recreation while retaining aspects of the area’s ranching character.Public access is comingFor now, the newly acquired land is not simply an open-to-everyone recreation area. Alpine County has said public access will begin after a comprehensive management plan is established. Once that happens, Park Ranch is expected to connect the Markleeville Campground with hiking trails beginning upstream at Hangman’s Bridge, creating a larger connected area for outdoor recreation.The result is a rare combination: a large working landscape moving into public ownership without losing its ranching character, while a free-flowing river, native fish habitat and a major wildlife passage remain protected for the future.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Woman, 89, told to remove her 25-year-old potted street garden
articles.summary: Katherine Hoskyns has tended the pots outside her St John's Wood home since the late 1990s.
articles.body:
An 89-year-old woman who has tended a street garden in St John's Wood in central London for more than 25 years has been told she may have to get rid of it after complaints.

Katharine Hoskyns was sent a removal notice by Westminster City Council in July, which told her to remove a bench and more than 20 plant pots on the pavement outside her home.

She said she created the garden after parking spaces were put in on the street, and has since grown geraniums, tomatoes and herbs there with help from neighbours.

"I was very upset and angry when I first got the letter, but then my family all rallied round and wrote a letter to the council and started this petition," she said.

The petition, started by her son, has gathered more than 190 signatures.

Katharine, a retired teacher who has lived in the area since the 1960s, said the garden gave her a reason to go outside.

"This space is important to me because I love gardening and it gives me plenty to do. I need an occupation in my retirement," she said.

"People come up and talk to me while I'm doing it, so it gives me a bit of a social life as well."

She said she had never seen anti-social behaviour at the site and disputed that the pots obstructed the pavement. She uses a walking frame and said she was able to pass them freely.

Westminster City Council said that unauthorised plant pots were subject to enforcement if they caused obstruction or were complained about.

Her neighbour Holly Bell-Stevens said the corner would lose its character if the pots went.

"We have this quiet oasis within the City of Westminster, and removing the pots means it would just become another concrete corner," she said.

"My children learned how to ride their bikes in this corner. We walk our dogs here. It cultivates a community and it touches everyone."

The deadline set out in the notice has passed and the garden has not been removed. Katharine said she expected to hear from the council again.

A Westminster City Council spokesperson said: "Following a series of resident complaints and attempts to resolve this dispute informally over several years, the council was, reluctantly, obliged to begin a formal process.

"Residents should be able to live without anti-social behaviour impacting on their lives. Moving this bench will help reduce the recent disturbance in the area.

"We remain hopeful that we can resolve the situation amicably."

The council said examples of anti-social behaviour around the bench had included drug taking and dumped rubbish, and that it hoped to work with Katharine to move the bench and pots to a more suitable location.

Residents said they would welcome a joint effort with the council over the future of the garden.

articles.title: San Diego nonprofit races to bring medical aid to flood-ravaged Nepal
articles.summary: A San Diego-based nonprofit, Sweeping Change, is mobilizing a medical team to assist victims of catastrophic flooding in Nepal following a massive glacier co...
articles.body:
SAN DIEGO (KUSI/FOX 5) — A San Diego nonprofit is stepping in to help victims of catastrophic flooding in Nepal as rescue crews race against time to find survivors.

A week after disaster struck, more than 1,000 people are dead and around 4,000 remain missing in the small South Asian country, and the human toll is growing by the day.

Haunting images show the aftermath of a massive glacier collapse on Aug. 26 along the Nepal–China border, which wiped out entire villages.

"You know you contact your friends, your colleagues to make sure they're safe," said Michael Sohmer, co-founder of Sweeping Change .

The people Sohmer knows personally there are not affected, but his nonprofit partner and Nepali native Hem Rai's family is.

"According to my niece her husband, uncles and aunts and two cousins washed away. Entire house. Pretty sad," said Rai, president and co-founder of Sweeping Change.

Sohmer, a retired clinical pharmacist and deputy commander for DMAT, a federal disaster response team, has spent years helping the Nepalese. He was just there in May.

Sometimes in the hardest moments, but always where the need is great.

"Even during regular times, I see a lot of people they have not enough medical need and also doesn't have enough education support," said Rai.

That calling is how the two first met. "I was just bebopping around Encinitas, and I saw earthquake relief on the window, and I walked in and I introduced myself," said Sohmer.

In 2015, Sohmer and Rai teamed up on a humanitarian mission to Nepal providing relief after a devastating earthquake. That included organizing doctors and nurses to join.

"We do crews, and of course medical supplies and all those tents, pots and pans, rice," said Rai.

Now their nonprofit is mobilizing a medical team to head back in early October for a two-week mission. "We'll triage and treat like we did in the earthquake," said Sohmer.

To provide the humanitarian aid and medication, they're raising funds. "All that money will go to the people of Nepal," said Sohmer.

They're optimistic roads will be accessible when they hit the ground in Nepal in the weeks ahead so they can get to the hardest-hit areas.

For the two friends, hope keeps them going, as they continue showing up for others. "I believe they will come together to build their country and they will rise again," said Rai.

Anyone interested in donating can visit their GoFundMe . They're also looking for volunteers with medical experience to reach out by emailing michael@sweepingchange.org.

articles.title: Runaway emu in Australia sparks police chase
articles.summary: Police said the "keen, young" officer who gave chase was enjoying his short-lived fame as the footage goes viral.
articles.body:
Footage of an Australian police officer chasing an emu down a country road has gone viral, with authorities using the light-hearted moment as a recruitment tool.

The flightless bird - native to Australia - was reported to police by locals in Nashdale, 270km (168 miles) west of Sydney, after it was seen wandering onto a road, posing a potential danger to traffic and itself.

Attempting to get the emu off the road, a young officer gave chase on foot but failed to catch his feathered target, despite speeding up at one point.

The video has attracted many comments on the "emu-sing" chase, with one viewer referencing a famed cartoon: "Look, it's the road runner, but that's not the coyote behind him".

On Tuesday, New South Wales police posted the footage on Facebook, saying the officer arrived at the scene to find the bird creating a "serious traffic hazard".

"Following a brief game of 'catch me if you can', the officer successfully moved the emu away from the roadway before it could ruffle any more feathers or cause a collision," police wrote in the post.

"It's not every day you find yourself conducting traffic management for an emu, but that's policing," adding that anyone looking for a career where "every day brings something new", becoming a police officer in regional areas was a good option.

Chief Inspector David Abercrombie from the Central West Police District said the "keen, young" officer who gave chase was enjoying his short-lived fame as the footage had been viewed almost 90,000 times.

Abercrombie said he was glad it wasn't him who had been called to the bizarre scene.

"If anyone asked me to chase an emu, it'd be more like watching a startled gazelle on Prozac," he told national broadcaster ABC. "My speed would not be up to scratch."

Police in regional and rural areas were often called about animals on the road, he said, but they usually involved livestock or kangaroos.

"It's the trials and tribulations of the life of a country cop," he said.

The footage has captivated many in recent days, with humorous observations posted online.

"Wait until it turns around and chases him. Then we'll see how fast he can run," joked one while another wrote: "At least that bird wasn't a flight risk."

And one person posted "Emu wars revisited", a reference to Australia's failed Emu War of 1932 when the military unsuccessfully attempted to cull thousands of the birds as they ravaged crops.

articles.title: Hundreds of firms are trying to access a new website that lets them study salvaged Russian weapons
articles.summary: Ukraine said over 430 firms have applied for access to TrophyLab, its new catalog of over 115 Russian weapons that also offers physical samples.
articles.body:
Ukraine says hundreds of firms have applied to join TrophyLab, its new catalog of Russian weapons.

The platform, launched in June, offers data on 115 types of captured Russian equipment.

Firms can access a database on these weapons or request a sample for study.

Ukraine's defense ministry said on Monday that over 430 firms have applied for access to its new catalog of seized Russian weapons and equipment, about two months after its launch announcement.

The online repository, called TrophyLab, contains data "for engineers, scientists, and defense technology manufacturers" on weapons such as the Russian T-90M main battle tank and the Kinzhal hypersonic missile .

More than 130 Ukrainian defense firms, as well as another 300 foreign companies, have submitted applications so far, the ministry said in a statement.

Ukrainian officials say the database, filled out by active combat units, intelligence and security services, and scientific institutions, offers over 225 blueprints, component analyses, and schematics to firms that pass a vetting process.

When the program was announced in late June, the defense ministry said it contained 115 samples of Russian drones , air-launched munitions, armored vehicles, and other equipment across 79 categories.

"Every missile, drone, and vehicle seized on the battlefield is now a source of knowledge for the free world," wrote Mykhailo Fedorov, the country's defense minister at the time.

TrophyLab also allows users to apply for a physical sample of a Russian weapon for "offline study" and to submit requests for information on specific types of Russian equipment.

According to the platform, firms will be able to destroy or disassemble some of these samples in their testing or inspections.

Eligibility to use TrophyLab is so far limited. Ukraine says it's only approving domestic manufacturers, certain scientific institutions, military units, and firms from partner countries that are already supplying its troops or screened by the defense ministry.

The move is part of Ukraine's concerted push to harvest data and information from its battlefield as a catalyst for weapons technologies at home and in the West.

The country has become a hotbed for defense startups and large, legacy manufacturers eager to trial their drones, robots, and electronic warfare systems in active combat — a service that Kyiv offers to friendly nations under its "Test in Ukraine" program.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has shared thousands of hours of frontline drone footage with allied nations, such as the UK and Germany, to help firms there train their AI systems.

articles.title: USS Abraham Lincoln: US sailors unwind in Thailand by shopping and bar-hopping
articles.summary: With military haircuts and moustaches, the US sailors stood out against the flip-flops of the usual Pattaya crowd, writes the BBC's Jonathan Head.
articles.body:
Far from hitting the bars and fleshpots of the Thai beach resort of Pattaya, in their first hours onshore most of the nearly 5,000 sailors from the USS Abraham Lincoln seemed determined to go shopping.

At the Hard Rock Hotel – one of two beachside hotels where they were able to stay off the ship – they hung around clutching their recent purchases. But perhaps, after a record 250 days confined inside a grey steel warship, the normality of a trip to the mall might have been just what they needed.

With their military haircuts, moustaches and navy t-shirts, they stood out against the usual Pattaya crowd in its flip-flops and beachwear.

Night, though, is where this resort city comes into its own and puts on a riotous spectacle of neon, noise and naughty bars.

Local businesses have been hoping to benefit from the sailors' nine months of unspent salary while at sea - but Pattaya's sex industry has been declared off-limits to the sailors, who have been reminded that prostitution is technically illegal in Thailand.

Conflict in the Middle East, where the USS Abraham Lincoln was last operating, has impacted business in Pattaya, with many of the tourists the city depends on choosing to stay at home.

But on Wednesday night, the city's most famous promenade, Walking Street, was very much open to the sailors, with a huge, illuminated sign at its entrance welcoming the crew of the US carrier.

By midnight some of the younger sailors there were so inebriated they had to prop each other up. Others edged nervously into the red-lit caverns of the go-go bars, with their gyrating and barely-clothed pole dancers.

Conversation over the pounding music was challenging. One older crew member told us they really needed the break.

"The news says we've been at sea for nine months. To be honest I've lost track of time", he said.

"It got boring. It's never big enough on board. It's big but it still feels like a boat, especially when you're sharing it with thousands of people." How long would it take them to get home to California? "Too long" he said.

Shakeira Fairfax, the mother of 25-year-old crew member Jada Fairfax, told Reuters there had been moments over the past few months when "morale was low".

She described the period after hostilities broke out in the Middle East as an "uncertain" and "scary" time.

"I just can't wait to see her smile. I can't wait to hear 'mum', I know that's the first thing she's gonna say," Fairfax added.

The crew have been well-drilled not to talk about conditions on board the USS Abraham Lincoln during its long combat deployment in the operation against Iran, which have been the subject of criticism back in the US.

Some sailors were wary of making any conversation at all. Others referred journalists' questions to their media teams. Visible everywhere in Pattaya were the men wearing t-shirts emblazoned with the letters SLG, or Shore Liaison Group.

It is their job to maintain discipline on land, to watch out for the crew members, some of whom are very young and inexperienced, and to co-ordinate with the local authorities during port calls.

US Naval Attache Kristopher Robinson did not answer questions from the BBC about activities that soldiers were banned from doing while in Pattaya, saying that "we're trying to give the sailors as much opportunity for rest as they can".

US personnel, he added, would "conduct themselves in accordance with US law, US naval regulations, and the laws of Thailand".

The decision by the USS Abraham Lincoln to stop in Pattaya makes a lot of sense. Port calls by the US Navy in Thailand, a long-standing treaty ally, are routine with well-established protocols.

It is also on the ship's route from the Gulf to California, giving the crew a chance to let off steam, and enjoy a break from the demands of life on board a warship.

If their stop in Thailand does the trick, any frustration they may feel over their unexpectedly long and tough mission may have dissipated by the time they get home.

articles.title: El Niño 'supersized' as countries race to prepare for extreme weather, UN warns
articles.summary: The WMO has warned that the natural weather phenomenon could bring disruption to global economies.
articles.body:
The world has entered a "danger zone of extreme weather" as the impacts of El Niño start to be felt globally, UN head António Guterres has warned.

The World Meteorological Organization (WMO) has released the latest data on the natural weather phenomenon showing it could be the strongest for more than 70 years and last until at least February 2027.

El Niño changes weather patterns around the world, pushing some regions into drought whilst others experience stronger typhoons and flooding.

Forecasters also say El Niño will boost temperatures in some places, coming on top of rising heat globally from human-induced climate change.

"El Niño is being supersized before our eyes. The science leaves no room for doubt: the planet is in uncharted waters, and those waters are heating up," Guterres said.

The BBC spoke with governments and scientists about the measures being taken globally to reduce the risk of deaths, displacement and environmental damage. Early warning systems have been strengthened and deployment of pre-emptive medical assistance, but the strength of this particular event has raised serious concerns particularly for vulnerable groups.

The WMO - a UN agency - said it has undertaken a "major mobilisation" to try to circulate its forecasts of potential extreme weather events, linked to El Niño, to as many communities as possible.

WMO Secretary-General Celeste Saulo warned: "El Niño has the potential to deliver a massive blow to communities and economies across the world."

El Niño is a natural weather phenomenon that develops in the Pacific Ocean and is linked to a change in wind patterns. It allows warm water to spread eastwards and releases heat into the atmosphere.

Sea temperatures in the central and eastern tropical Pacific have risen sharply in recent months - a clear sign of a strengthening El Niño.

In the Pacific's key monitoring region, surface temperatures have been well over 2C above average in recent weeks, putting it on track to be declared a "very strong" event.

But it is expected to surpass even that marker. Monthly sea surface temperatures could get close to 4C above average, forecasts suggest.

This would make it the strongest El Niño since at least 1950, by potentially a large margin.

Temperatures are even more exceptional below the surface of the Pacific - in places more than 8C above average.

Above-normal sea temperatures are also expected in other parts of the world including the Indian Ocean, tropical Atlantic and around parts of the Australian coast.

With its rich marine life, changes in ocean heat are of particular concern to Australia.

It has been plagued by marine heatwaves in recent years - driven by climate change.

El Niño is a natural phenomenon, but it tends to bring the kind of extreme heat which also drives those disasters, Dr Alistair Hobday, chief researcher at Australia's science agency, told the BBC.

This year, marine heatwave forecasts indicate the Great Barrier Reef will be spared the worst of the conditions, giving coral there more time to recover.

"[But] Southern Australia is getting slammed," said Hobday.

Last time a marine heatwave hit South Australia and Tasmania, there were starving penguins, fish kills, suffocating algae outbreaks, and jellyfish invasions.

Australia has recently introduced early warning systems for marine crises - this gives time for financial relief for fisheries to be established, relocation of crucial species and increased coral monitoring.

But this event is shaping up to be unprecedented - and Hobday admits he is quite worried.

Reduced rainfall brings drought and trade disruption

While the impacts on global weather are likely to be felt well into 2027, the WMO expects significant changes in rainfall patterns over the next few months.

Drier-than-usual conditions are forecast across large areas of South East Asia, Central America and northern parts of South America, increasing the risk of droughts and wildfires.

On Thursday, the number of vessels passing through the Panama Canal will be reduced by more than 10% in anticipation of lower rainfall.

About 14,000 ships per year use the artificial waterway - as well as being a crucial route for global trade, it is also a key source of income for Panama, bringing in about $3bn (£2.2bn) a year.

Indonesia is racing to contain wildfires that have burned more than 107,000 hectares of land nationwide this dry season. Like some other parts of South East Asia, it is facing a longer season this year.

A resident in Central Kalimantan told BBC News Indonesia he had been experiencing wildfires "for more than a month".

"The smoke has become quite thick. When we step outside, our eyes start to sting. The smell of the smoke is also quite strong," said Darwin Romy.

Authorities have said they are deploying cloud-seeding aircraft to trigger rains to extinguish these fires, and its government has promised resources to contain the fire and arrested dozens over allegations of using it to clear land.

Thousands of miles away, China is expecting seven typhoons to make landfall in this year alone – something the country's experts have said is linked to the effects of a super El Niño.

In July alone, China experienced three typhoons - Bavi, Noul and Maysak - which left dozens dead.

And in August, more than 1m people were forced to evacuate their homes as Typhoon Dolphin hit – bringing heavy rains and strong winds.

Similarly, wetter-than-average weather is expected in parts of eastern Africa, southern Brazil and the southern US, raising the chances of flooding.

"We are already seeing disruption and devastation from droughts and floods and we expect these impacts to increase as El Niño intensifies," said Prof Celeste Saulo, secretary general of the WMO.

This is all happening on top of long-term human-caused warming, making the impacts potentially more intense. Some scientists believe climate change could even be making El Niño events stronger, but this is not yet certain.

Peru is particularly vulnerable to El Niño, as its coastline borders the eastern Pacific.

Parts of the country, along with Ecuador and parts of Brazil, have previously experienced increased rainfall, resulting in flash flooding and landslides, particularly in urban centres where the water is less able to drain away.

Miguel Aréstegui, climate resilience lead at Practical Action, which helps countries prepare for extreme weather, said "we are significantly concerned, but that concern needs to translate into preparedness rather than alarm."

He said Practical Action had been working with partners over recent years to make sure the public had better access to early warning systems, including sharing information on river levels, flood risks and weather forecasts.

At the end of last month, the US announced it was deploying the vessel USNS Comfort to the Peruvian coast to provide additional medical assistance and technical equipment for when El Niño reaches its peak.

However, Aréstegui said El Niño "does not arrive in a vacuum". There are bigger, structural issues that make these events worse and which take much longer to resolve such as "housing in exposed areas, fragile water and sanitation systems, and a weak healthcare system", he said.

articles.title: With a wary eye on Russia, Finland runs Europe's largest civil defense exercise since WWII
articles.summary: In a civil defense shelter hewn into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and...
articles.body:
KUOPIO, Finland (AP) — In a civil defense shelter hewn into rock, behind doors designed to withstand a nuclear or biological attack, two Finnish conscripts wearing hazmat suits and breathing masks are measuring radiation levels as they take part in an exercise to turn a cave into a place of safety for thousands of people.

Inside, in what is normally a sports hall, hundreds of people are sleeping overnight on trestle beds.

More than 2,000 people including volunteers and students are taking part in the biggest civil defense exercise in Europe since the end of World War II. In the scenario, critical infrastructure in the central Finnish city of Kuopio, including power and water, has been disrupted by cyberattacks and there's the threat of missile strikes from Finland's neighbor, Russia.

The goal is for local authorities and ordinary people to rehearse what they would do if they came under attack for real.

But while underground bunkers and shelters may offer some protection from missiles, they are no defense against the campaign of sabotage and disruption that Western officials say Russia is carrying out across Europe. That has involved setting fires , attacking water facilities and power stations , and sending drones for sabotage into European Union airspace.

Finland's border with Russia stretches more than 830 miles (1,300 kilometers) from the Baltic Sea up to the Arctic Circle. In 2024, along with Sweden, Finland joined NATO, following Russian President Vladimir Putin's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Until then, Finns were prepared to defend themselves against Russia largely alone.

Finland's defense, said retired Army Colonel Asko Muhonen, relies not only on the military but on the "mindset" of ordinary Finns who are ready to take responsibility for their country's security.

Muhonen, who organized the exercise in Kuopio, said that comes partly from the system of conscription which continued in Finland, even after the collapse of the Soviet Union.

Not everyone is happy about doing national service but "it's our duty to serve and protect this country like people have before us. That's why we have our independence," said Jyry Pietikainen, 23, a conscript who was taught how to run the Kuopio shelter overnight.

Finland also needs to learn lessons from Ukraine, Muhonen said.

While the biggest shelter in Kuopio can fit 7,000 people, Ukrainians sometimes only have a few minutes to run to a subway station or underground parking lot. That means people need a shelter they can reach easily that offers some form of protection — not necessarily one that can withstand a nuclear attack, he said.

Dmytro Untila, 20, a Ukrainian student at the university in Kuopio, was at home in Odesa when Russian missiles struck his city on Feb. 24, 2022, the first day of the war. He sheltered in the entrance hall of his building because he didn't have anywhere else to go, he said.

Training for such a situation would have definitely helped in Ukraine, he said, "because nobody knew this could happen."

The biggest threat to energy infrastructure in the Kuopio region is heavy snowfall, storms and bad weather, said Juha Räsänen, CEO at the Savon Voima electricity company.

But since the invasion of Ukraine, and the company's decision to stop buying Russian biofuel, the number of cyberattacks against the network has significantly increased, Räsänen said.

Last year, engineers also found at least 10 stickers placed on particularly vulnerable parts of the energy network infrastructure. Other energy companies in Finland have also found them and don't know where they came from, he said.

"If there was an explosion at that point, it could destroy a whole dam," Räsänen said. Drones have also been spotted over power lines but those responsible have not been identified, he said.

It is not possible to guard against all threats, Räsänen said, which is why it's important people are prepared to look after themselves without help for at least 72 hours — if the power supply goes out, or if water becomes undrinkable.

The Finnish Security and Intelligence Service said it investigated "a wide range of observations" and found nothing of concern.

Since 2022, people have been more vigilant because of the security situation and therefore have reported things like reflective stickers related to land survey works, it said in a statement. Drone sightings, it said, have "largely been explained by everyday occurrences."

"Small things are happening all the time," including Russian jamming of GPS signals, said Vuokko Lahtinen, 32, who was visiting a sauna in Kuopio.

For that reason, "the best defense of Finland is to make it not worth attacking," she said.

That relies on the country's military and defense forces but also Finnish people who feel like "we have something we want to fight for," she said.

In Finland, she said, there is a "general feeling of responsibility," which has grown out of local community groups and even initiatives such as recycling.

"On a very simple daily level, if you do things that matter, then it has a butterfly-wing effect," Lahtinen said.

Finland fought several wars with the Soviet Union

In its wars with the Soviet Union, Finland lost around 11% of its territory, and more than 400,000 people, around 12% of the population, fled their homes from an area that is now in western Russia.

At Kuopio's veterans' museum, Risto Mönkkönen, 95, showed AP a piece of paper on which he had written down the dates the city was bombed and who died.

"I cannot forget it," he said explaining how, as a child, he and his father ran into a shelter just as a bomb hit, killing five of his father's friends.

Pirkko Naukkarinen, 102, recalled how, aged 16, she worked in a field kitchen by the front lines, sometimes sharing dugouts with soldiers and diving for cover in ditches as the Soviet air force attacked the retreating Finnish army.

Aili Toivanen, 92, told AP she was forced to leave her home twice over the various wars. Both times, her family was told by Finnish soldiers that they had one hour to pack their belongings.

The first time, she looked back and saw her home burning — set on fire by Finnish soldiers who did not want to leave anything behind, she said. The second time, she said, the Soviet air force bombed the family's departing train and they jumped out, hiding in ditches before they took refuge in Kuopio.

When Putin invaded Ukraine in 2022, she said, with tears in her eyes, that she worried she would have to leave her home for a third time.

Finns feel their country is worth fighting for

At the shelter in Kuopio, thousands of people filed in, including schoolchildren and university students.

"Kids would need to know this, because they might have to do something alone. The adults can't always help," said Amanda Hill, 11, whose school studied in the shelter for the day.

Sitting on the floor of the shelter with his fellow conscripts, Pietikainen explained why it's not crazy to practice what happens in a crisis.

"We're Finns, so we're kind of pessimistic about life in a way," but history shows what can happen with Russia, he said.

When it comes to the threats from Moscow, Muhonen said, "don't believe what they say but observe what they do."

articles.title: World’s richest person Elon Musk once forgot his wife’s Christmas gift; when ex-wife Talulah Riley recalled how he went barefoot into the snow and returned with flowers instead
articles.summary: Rest of World News: Elon Musk once forgot to buy his then-wife Talulah Riley a Christmas present. What happened later that night, however, was something she remembered ye.
articles.body: Elon Musk once forgot to buy his then-wife Talulah Riley a Christmas present. What happened later that night, however, was something she remembered years afterwards. Riley, the British actress who married Musk twice, recalled the incident in the BBC documentary The Elon Musk Show, which was first broadcast in 2022. She said the couple were living in Boulder, Colorado, at the time and there was heavy snow outside.According to Riley, Musk realised he had forgotten her Christmas gift and told her that it was not because he did not love her, but because he was overwhelmed and his “brain” was exploding.She said she did not make much of it. But later that night, Musk got out of bed and disappeared. Two hours later, he returned with flowers.Musk went out barefoot in the snowRiley recalled that Musk had gone outside wearing only a T-shirt and shorts and was barefoot. According to her account, he walked around Boulder, dug through the snow and picked flowers before returning with a small bouquet. “He'd walked all over Boulder and came back with a little bouquet of picked flowers,” Riley recalled in the documentary. She said Musk then told her: “I just wanted to show you how much I loved you.”Riley said Musk was far from “cold and emotionless”For Riley, the incident was more than a story about a forgotten Christmas present. She used it to challenge the public image of Musk as someone who is detached or unemotional. In the documentary, Riley described him as “the most emotional person I know” and said the idea that he was cold and emotionless was far removed from her experience of him.She also described a certain innocence in him and said he felt emotions very deeply. The Christmas incident came during a period when Musk was dealing with intense pressure around his businesses. Riley recalled that he was under enormous stress at the time and that she was concerned about his health.The documentary looked at Musk's rise through interviews with people who knew him, including family members, friends and associates. The series also covered the period when SpaceX was fighting for survival and Tesla was struggling to establish itself.Musk and Talulah Riley married twiceRiley and Musk's relationship had its own twists. The couple first married in 2010 and divorced in 2012. They later reconciled and married again in 2013, before divorcing for a second time in 2016.Despite their relationship ending, Riley has spoken positively about Musk in the years since their marriages ended. She has referred to him as a “perfect ex-husband”, and has also publicly described his emotional side. The flower story is one of the more personal memories she has shared about their relationship.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Sergey Brin’s $450 million superyacht Dragonfly has been forced to dock at a Spanish Navy cruise berth, and the reason is ...
articles.summary: Tech News News: Google co-founder Sergey Brin's superyacht Dragonfly is so large that even a routine fuel stop becomes a commercial-scale operation. Measuring 466 fee.
articles.body: Google co-founder Sergey Brin's superyacht Dragonfly is so large that even a routine fuel stop becomes a commercial-scale operation. Measuring 466 feet (142.1 meters), the Lürssen-built yacht is too large for the kind of fuel pump found at an ordinary marina, forcing it to rely on Gibraltar's industrial bunkering infrastructure instead. Delivered in 2024 and valued at approximately $450 million, the yacht's sheer size recently forced it to dock at a Spanish Navy cruise berth.​In a recent YouTube video from the channel Gibraltar Yachting, Dragonfly can be seen berthed alongside Gibraltar's commercial-scale bunkering terminal, with shoreside fuel tanks towering behind it. The scene offers a glimpse of what refuelling a yacht of this size actually involves. It looks less like a stop at a luxury marina and more like a visit from a small ship to a working fuel port.​A fuel stop measured in hours​The scale of Dragonfly becomes clearer when you consider the fuel figures. The Gibraltar bunkering operation, run through Gib Oil's Western Arm terminal, can deliver fuel directly through its pipe system at rates of up to 80 metric tons per hour. Even at that rate, Dragonfly would take about 13 hours to tank up fully, depending on the amount required.​Gibraltar's fuel infrastructure includes 18 tanks with around 3,200 metric tons of marine gas oil and automotive gas oil storage, along with a separate facility capable of storing another 13,350 metric tons of marine gas oil. The operation also has barges available for vessels refuelling at anchor or requiring different fuel grades.​For Dragonfly, even a partial 500-metric-ton refill would be substantial. That amount translates to roughly 581,000 litres of diesel and could cost approximately $690,000 to $720,000 at indicative Gibraltar marine gas oil prices of $1,380 to $1,440 per metric ton.​At the maximum pumping rate, filling that amount would take about 6¼ hours. A 1,000-metric-ton uplift would mean around 1.16 million litres, a bill of roughly $1.38 million to $1.44 million, and about 12½ hours of pumping.​By comparison, using conventional road tankers would be far less practical. A 1.16-million-litre delivery would require roughly 58 truckloads, or around 60 tankers when rounded, and could take about two days using 20,000-litre fuel trucks.​Why Gibraltar, and why the Navy berth​Gibraltar's Ocean Village Marina can accommodate superyachts measuring up to around 100 meters. Still, the 142-meter Dragonfly is too large for that facility, forcing it to use the port's commercial-scale North Mole facilities instead, including the Spanish Navy cruise berth where it was recently docked.​Gibraltar is particularly convenient for a vessel of this size because it sits at the gateway between the Atlantic and Mediterranean. More than 60,000 vessels pass through the Strait each year, and Gibraltar functions as a bunkering hub with competitive fuel pricing and infrastructure built for vessels much larger than those found in conventional yacht marinas.​Dragonfly's Gibraltar visit also appears to have been an operational stop rather than a leisure destination. AIS records show the yacht travelled roughly 463 nautical miles from Palma de Mallorca toward Gibraltar before continuing its journey. Its latest reported destination is Alcudia, Spain, according to MarineTraffic, with the yacht heading back toward the Balearics.​A floating complex that still needs fuel​Dragonfly is not simply a large hull with lavish cabins. The 9,408-gross-ton yacht runs on a diesel-electric hybrid propulsion system powered by two MAN 16V28/33D diesel engines, each roughly the size of a semi-truck, weighing 44 tons and generating 9,760 hp. Together, they propel the vessel to a reported top speed of 24 knots. Germán Frers designed the yacht, with Nauta Design responsible for its interiors and social spaces. It also includes a dedicated business deck, reflecting Brin's apparent desire to work while travelling.​Across its five decks are the kinds of facilities expected on a yacht of this scale, including a glass-bottom swimming pool, spa, gym, games room, cinema, beauty salon, elevators, galleys, refrigeration and laundry facilities. It also carries navigation and communications systems, water-making and waste-treatment equipment, and infrastructure supporting tenders and helicopter operations.​The hybrid propulsion setup can make the vessel more efficient and quieter, but it does not make Dragonfly fuel-independent. Its diesel engines remain essential to generating the energy needed to move the yacht and support its onboard hotel load.​Get the latest technology news and updates. Download the TOI App.

articles.title: ‘No record’: Podcaster’s claim reignites row over CJP founder’s BU degree; Dipke hits back with video
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: A fresh controversy has erupted over Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke’s educational credentials after podcaster Prakhar G.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: A fresh controversy has erupted over Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) founder Abhijeet Dipke’s educational credentials after podcaster Prakhar Gupta said one of his friends who studied at Boston University could not find a record of Dipke’s graduation there.The claim was made during an episode of The Prakhar Gupta Xperience podcast featuring climate activist Sonam Wangchuk.Gupta said one of his close friends had studied at Boston University and had been actively involved in supporting the CJP-led protest at Jantar Mantar.“One of my best friends went to Boston University. It is also Abhijeet’s college,” Gupta said during the podcast.He said his friend had participated in the protests and produced media content in support of the movement.Gupta claimed that about a month later, his friend began looking into Dipke’s educational credentials and allegedly found no record of him graduating from Boston University.“He has gone down the rabbit hole of checking up Abhijeet’s education credentials and found there is no record of him graduating from Boston University,” Gupta said.Dipke, however, responded to the claim on X, appearing to mock the suggestion that his graduation could not be verified.“Not my fault that his friends were not invited at BU COM Grad events,” Dipke wrote, while sharing a video appearing to show him at an event associated with Boston University’s College of Communication graduate community.The video was a screen recording of a story posted by an Instagram account identified as “BU COM Grad, Student Council”.The latest allegation comes despite Boston University itself having published material identifying Dipke as a graduate.In a June 2026 article, Boston University’s College of Communication described Dipke as a “COM grad” and said he had completed his master’s in public relations from the university the previous year.The university article also carried an interview with Dipke in which he discussed how his studies at BU influenced the communication strategy behind the CJP campaign.Dipke has previously maintained that he studied at Boston University and earned a master’s degree in public relations. He has also said his education was financed through a Boston University scholarship and an education loan.Amid the controversy, Dipke had earlier said he was willing to produce his degree and other documents to establish his educational credentials.The dispute has now resurfaced as Dipke and the CJP leadership face increasing scrutiny over their backgrounds and political ambitions following the movement’s prolonged protests over examination-related issues.Sonam Wangchuk on Dipke’s political ambitionsThe same podcast also featured Wangchuk discussing Dipke and other CJP organisers, including their possible political ambitions.Wangchuk said he believed Dipke and his fellow organisers appeared to have political aspirations, although they had not explicitly told him about any such plans. He said there was nothing inherently wrong with political ambitions as long as the CJP remained a non-party platform.“Political ambition is very normal,” Wangchuk said, adding that he did not care about the organisers’ past political connections and had no problem with their present or future political aspirations.Wangchuk also said the organisers were not necessarily acting entirely selflessly and described them as “well meaning”, “quite skilled” and “above average”. He cautioned that their political aspirations should not turn the CJP platform itself into a vehicle for any political party.He said the organisers could eventually join an existing political party or form one of their own, but should preserve CJP as a “neutral, apolitical pressure group”.The comments came days before the Supreme Court quashed 127 FIRs filed against student protesters in five states in connection with the CJP agitation.Following assurances given before the court, CJP called off its proposed September 5 march from India Gate to Delhi Police headquarters.You Can Also Check: Gold Rate in Delhi | Silver Rate in Delhi | Bank Holidays in Delhi | Public Holidays in Delhi | Delhi AQI | Weather in Delhi | Petrol Price in Delhi | Diesel Price in Delhi | CNG Price in Delhi | LPG Price in DelhiStay updated with the latest Delhi news. articles.title: Two Amazon delivery drivers carried an 85-year-old Kentucky woman’s printer inside; minutes later she stopped breathing and they performed CPR that helped save her life
articles.summary: US News: An ordinary delivery turned into a medical emergency for two Amazon delivery drivers in Covington, Kentucky, on Tuesday. Eric Bunzow and Shawn Beam ha.
articles.body: An ordinary delivery turned into a medical emergency for two Amazon delivery drivers in Covington, Kentucky, on Tuesday. Eric Bunzow and Shawn Beam had just delivered a printer to an 85-year-old woman when she suddenly collapsed.According to Fox 19, Bunzow and Beam, who are longtime friends and Amazon Delivery Service Partner drivers, had carried the printer inside the woman’s home. After the delivery, she invited them to see the view from her balcony. Few moments later, she said she was feeling dizzy.“She said, ‘Oh, you ain’t seen nothing, let’s go look at the balcony,’” Bunzow said. “As we were walking, she said, ‘Young man, I feel a little dizzy.’ I said, ‘Here, hold my hand, I’ll set you down.’ When she grabbed my hand, she collapsed.”The woman fell into Beam, who helped prevent her from hitting her head. The two drivers then realised that she was not breathing and immediately began responding to the emergency.Drivers respond quicklyBeam, who has training in safety response, began the Heimlich manoeuvre after the woman collapsed. At the same time, Bunzow called paramedics for help. “I said, ‘Eric, she’s not breathing.’ He said, ‘What?’ I said, ‘She’s not breathing!’” Beam reacalled.Bunzow said he recognised the symptoms because of a previous experience. The emergency also reminded him of the death of his mother, who died in March.“My mom passed away in March, and then to watch her ... she died on us ... like he said, we were at the right place at the right time,” Bunzow said.The drivers continued helping the woman while waiting for emergency responders. Paramedics arrived within five minutes.Son says help came in timeThe woman’s son, James, said the actions of the two drivers may have made a major difference because they were already inside the home when his mother collapsed.He said emergency responders might not have arrived in time without Bunzow and Beam being there and acting quickly.“The fact they were there and made quick actions- we’re not planning a funeral,” James said. “We are celebrating my mom being around for more time.”Drivers plan to returnBunzow and Beam said they plan to visit the 85-year-old woman again. They remembered the balcony and the view she had wanted to show them before the emergency. “Eventually, we want to see that view and make sure that she’s doing okay,” Bunzow said.Beam also said he hoped they could return and spend some time with her on the patio. “Just sit on the patio with her and be like, ‘Look at this, amazing,’” Beam said. “I bet there’s a nice breeze coming through there right now.”Amazon praises Amazon said Bunzow and Beam’s actions reflected the response and care expected from its Delivery Service Partner community.“We’re proud of Eric and Shawn for their courage and quick response in helping a resident experiencing a medical emergency while they were out on their delivery route,” Amazon said in a statement.The company said the two drivers deliver for a Delivery Service Partner in its network and described their actions as an example of drivers supporting the communities they serve.“Eric and Shawn deliver for a Delivery Service Partner in our network, and their actions reflect the compassion and character we see across the DSP community, where drivers regularly go above and beyond to support the communities they serve,” Amazon said.The company also said its thoughts were with the woman and her family as she continued her recovery.Catch the latest World News and Live updates.
